entities.name: Académie Française
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Académie Française, established in 1635 under the auspices of Cardinal Richelieu, stands as the pre-eminent institution for the preservation and promotion of the French language. Located in Paris, it was conceived during a time when France sought to assert cultural supremacy in Europe and to standardize the French language amid regional dialects. The Académie not only codified rules of grammar and style but also played a crucial role in defining French identity in the context of the Enlightenment and the subsequent rise of national languages across Europe.

In its formative years, the Académie introduced the first official French dictionary in 1694, which was a hallmark of linguistic scholarship at the time. The institution convened regularly to discuss matters of language, literature, and culture, producing literary awards that encouraged the flourishing of French literature. Its influence extended beyond France, as the standards it set were adopted by Francophone writers and scholars worldwide, establishing a linguistic benchmark that continues to have a lasting impact on French language education.

The legacy of the Académie Française is evident in its ongoing role as a guardian of the French language, influencing educational systems and cultural policies in France and other French-speaking regions. Its members, known as "Les Immortels," have included prominent figures such as Voltaire, Racine, and Hugo, whose works have become integral to the Western literary canon. The institution’s efforts to modernize and adapt the language to contemporary usage ensure its relevance in an ever-evolving linguistic landscape.
